History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma presents with 2-day history of worsening wheeze and exertional/ nocturnal shortness of breath after heavy dust exposure while cleaning.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheezing and shortness of breath.  
• Onset: Began ~2 days ago about 1 hour after cleaning dusty carpet.  
• Course: Gradually worsening; more pronounced at night; difficulty completing sentences during conversations today.  
• Aggravating factors: None specifically noted beyond dust exposure.  
• Relieving factors: None tried; has not used inhaler or other medication.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies chest pain or pleuritic pain; denies dizziness/vertigo. Eating and drinking adequate (≈4–5 glasses water/day).  
• Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, no dizziness, no documented fever, cough, sputum, or infection symptoms.

Past Medical History:
• Childhood asthma – intermittent adult symptoms with prolonged running; previously treated with inhalers and steroids.  
• Seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) – untreated.  
• No other chronic illnesses discussed.

Medications:
• Asthma inhaler (type/dose/route/frequency not documented); last used “a couple of months ago.”  
• No current antihistamine.  
Allergies: No known drug allergies; possible dust allergy suspected but not formally diagnosed.

Social History:
• Lives close to GP surgery (“minutes’ drive”).  
• Occupational, smoking, alcohol, and substance history not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not performed in teleconsult.  
• General/respiratory/other exam findings: Not performed.

Investigations:
• None performed.  
• Planned: Pulse oximetry and further assessment at GP clinic.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected asthma exacerbation vs. acute allergic reaction to dust
  • Plan:
    – Urgent in-person GP review today for pulse oximetry and respiratory assessment.  
    – Consider prescribing/ administering short-acting bronchodilator (patient has an inhaler at home) and oral corticosteroids if objective findings confirm exacerbation.  
    – Trial over-the-counter oral antihistamine prior to review if available.  
    – Provide referral letter via app summarizing consult.

Issue 2: Under-treated seasonal allergic rhinitis / possible dust allergy
  • Plan:
    – Initiate or resume regular non-sedating antihistamine; GP to advise formulation and dosing.  
    – Discuss environmental control measures for dust exposure at follow-up.

General Plan items:
  • Advise patient to seek emergency care (call emergency services) if she develops severe breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, chest pain, or dizziness.  
  • Encourage hydration; monitor symptoms.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Detailed vital signs, physical exam, peak flow/pulse oximetry values, full medication list, smoking/alcohol history, formal allergy list.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional audio dropout but key clinical details understandable.
